newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels extend control over south.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels extend control over south.

text.p: Anti-government forces took control of the major southern Albanian town of Berat without a fight after the army abandoned it en masse, a spokesman for the rebels said on Monday.

Control of Berat put most of southern Albania in the grip of rebels demanding President Sali Berisha's resignation and ignoring the weekend pact he signed with the opposition for a national unity government and new elections.

The spokesman said the army moved out of its barracks in Berat, one of Albania's oldest towns, soon after state television broadcast parts of the meeting showing the president and political parties clinching the accord.
A doctor at the hospital in Berat said one person had been killed and 20 slightly injured in random shooting, but there were no clashes.
Shots reverberated throughout the town and surrounding hills and most residents appeared to have remained indoors to avoid the risk of being hit by stray bullets.
The spokesman said rebels supported the idea of a caretaker government as proposed during Sunday's agreement in Tirana.
But they insisted on the resignation of Berisha, whom they blamed for allowing pyramid schemes to flourish before collapsing with the savings of hundreds of thousands.
"We dont trust him any more," said Sokol, one of the rebels. "He deserves to be hanged by his tongue."
Rebels accuse the president either of direct links to the schemes or of failing to intervene to stop their development and warn unwary investors of the risks.

"The schemes were created by the government to steal money from us," said Afrim, another rebel fighter. "If the government had given us back the money that was stolen, nothing like this would have happened in Albania."
Berisha was meeting in Tirana with political parties to determine the make-up of the interim governmet pending elections in June.

At Berat's deserted barracks, armed civilians guarding the gate said they had taken control of the building to prevent weapons falling into the hands of children as has happened in other towns in rebel hands.
For the first time in over a week there were no army roadblocks on the road south of the Shkumbini River that divides the Balkan country into north and south.
The only army tanks visible were clustered in a group just south of the river apparently guarding the road north to Tirana and east to government held-towns like Elbasan.
A policeman manning the last roadblock on the road south in Lushnje, 20 km (12 miles) south of the river, waved in derision when asked about the army.
"What army? There is no army around here," he said. "We are the only ones left and we're thinking of pulling out. We have to protect ourselves."
Berat's 40,000 residents were once solidly behind Berisha and his government but public opinion shifted sharply after the collapse of five pyramid schemes in January.
Enraged investors in January set fire to official buildings in the town, including the town hall, the police station and the prosecutor's office.
